items.text:
eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise

20th October 2026

The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

To demonstrate that the keys are compromised, the original reporter Wayne signed the following message with the private key of each of the eight intermediate CAs and reported it to the Root Program Teams on the 17th of October:

We have a problem here - Wayne

proof.zip contains the message, and for each intermediate the certificate, its public key and a signature on the message. To verify with OpenSSL:

openssl x509 -in EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.crt.pem -noout -pubkey | diff - EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.pub.pem
openssl dgst -sha384 -verify EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.pub.pem -signature EM-DV-TLS-CA-G3B.sig message.txt

The root programs and many downstream trust stores have taken action to protect their users. The certificates have been blocked in Firefox and Chrome since the 17th of October, in Apple devices since the 19th and on Microsoft platforms since the 20th.

The issue was responsibly disclosed to downstream trust stores on the 19th of October. Many have already released updates or are in the process of releasing updates.

An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service.

This has already been remediated by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome for their users through their tools for distributing revocation information such as OneCRL, CRLite and CRLSets.

The CA has also revoked the compromised intermediate certificates. However, many other clients do not consume revocation information and require software updates to ensure they no longer trust the compromised intermediates.

Intermediate CA

Chains to

Result

Run again

To check curl or other command-line clients, run:

curl https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/
curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

A certificate error means the client does not trust the compromised intermediates.

To check a trust store offline, chains.zip contains the certificate chain served by each of the twelve hosts above in PEM format, with instructions for verifying them with OpenSSL.

impacted-intermediates.json lists the eight intermediates and their Sectigo cross-signs. roots.json lists the roots they chain to.

The private keys for the intermediate certificates were incorrectly generated by the CA. This means that anyone can recover them from the certificates.

This would have been possible since the certificates were created in April 2025. There are no entries in the certificate transparency logs for these intermediates in that period, indicating that CT-enforcing clients like Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari could not have been attacked.

However, many clients outside of the browser ecosystem do not enforce Certificate Transparency. We do not know if attackers exploited the flawed key generation to target these clients.

Further technical information about the cause is captured in the initial incident report in Mozilla's bug tracker.

Please see this thread in Mozilla's dev-security-policy forum.

Users should update their browsers and operating systems to the latest versions as soon as possible.

Add more at github.com/galadran/we-have-a-problem.com.

macOS blocks the compromised intermediates, but the built-in /usr/bin/curl verifies certificates against /etc/ssl/cert.pem without checking revocation, and that file has not been updated. To remove the affected roots from it, run:

sudo cp /etc/ssl/cert.pem /etc/ssl/cert.pem.bak &&
awk '/^(###|===) /{skip=0}
/^=== .*\/CN=(AAA Certificate Services|emSign ECC Root CA - G3)$/{skip=1}
!skip' /etc/ssl/cert.pem.bak | sudo tee /etc/ssl/cert.pem > /dev/null

Until a distribution ships an updated ca-certificates package, expert users can distrust the affected roots in the system trust store. This is NOT recommended for ordinary users.

On Debian and Ubuntu, run as root:

sed -i \
-e 's|^mozilla/emSign_ECC_Root_CA_-_G3.crt|!&|' \
-e 's|^mozilla/Comodo_AAA_Services_root.crt|!&|' \
/etc/ca-certificates.conf && update-ca-certificates

On Alpine, run as root:

apk add ca-certificates &&
sed -i -e 's|^mozilla/emSign_ECC_Root_CA_-_G3.crt|!&|' \
/etc/ca-certificates.conf && update-ca-certificates

On Fedora, RHEL, CentOS Stream, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux and Amazon Linux 2023, run as root:

d=/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/blocklist; [ -d $d ] || d=/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/blacklist
trust extract --overwrite --format=pem-bundle \
--filter='pkcs11:object=Comodo%20AAA%20Services%20root;type=cert' \
$d/Comodo_AAA_Services_root.pem &&
trust extract --overwrite --format=pem-bundle \
--filter='pkcs11:object=emSign%20ECC%20Root%20CA%20-%20G3;type=cert' \
$d/emSign_ECC_Root_CA_-_G3.pem &&
update-ca-trust

On openSUSE and SLES, run as root:

d=/etc/pki/trust/blocklist; [ -d $d ] || d=/etc/pki/trust/blacklist
trust extract --format=pem-bundle \
--filter='pkcs11:object=Comodo%20AAA%20Services%20root;type=cert' \
$d/Comodo_AAA_Services_root.pem &&
trust extract --format=pem-bundle \
--filter='pkcs11:object=emSign%20ECC%20Root%20CA%20-%20G3;type=cert' \
$d/emSign_ECC_Root_CA_-_G3.pem &&
update-ca-certificates

On Arch Linux, run as root:

trust extract --format=pem-bundle \
--filter='pkcs11:object=emSign%20ECC%20Root%20CA%20-%20G3;type=cert' \
/etc/ca-certificates/trust-source/blocklist/emSign_ECC_Root_CA_-_G3.pem &&
update-ca-trust

On NixOS, add to your configuration:

security.pki.caCertificateBlacklist = [
"Comodo AAA Services root"
"emSign ECC Root CA - G3"
];

On NetBSD 10 and later, run as root:

certctl untrust /usr/share/certs/mozilla/all/emSign_ECC_Root_CA_-_G3.pem &&
certctl untrust /usr/share/certs/mozilla/all/Comodo_AAA_Services_root.pem

On FreeBSD 14 or later, run the following commands as root:

cp /etc/ssl/certs/14bc7599.0 /usr/share/certs/untrusted/14bc7599.pem
cp /etc/ssl/certs/ee64a828.0 /usr/share/certs/untrusted/ee64a828.pem
certctl rehash

Site published by Dennis Jackson. The source is on GitHub and PRs are welcome.

items.title: Ofcom concedes defeat in 4chan case
items.author: iamnothere
items.summary:
Insofar as a political organization like Ofcom is even capable of admitting defeat, it did so in the 4chan enforcement today.

In testimony before the Commons
items.text:
Insofar as a political organization like Ofcom is even capable of admitting defeat, it did so in the 4chan enforcement today.

In testimony before the Commons Digital, Culture, Media, and Sport Committee, Ofcom admitted it knows its jurisdiction ends where a foreign court’s jurisdiction begins.

“We won’t be able to recover every single fine on online safety. If foreign courts decide to try and get in our way, there will be a point at which we have to accept that we won’t be able to recover that money.”

– Dame Melanie Dawes, Chief Executive, Ofcom

Guido Fawkes characterizes this admission thus: “Ofcom Admits Defeat.”

Guido is right. American courts have, by now, provided their preliminary view on the likelihood of Ofcom’s enforcement powers being successful in U.S. courts – the obiter dicta in 4chan v. Ofcom, the opinion in the case we filed against Ofcom in the federal District Court for the District of Columbia a little over a year ago.

Those dicta made it awfully clear that Ofcom can expect a very chilly reception in an American courtroom if it ever tries to enforce its fines in the United States. By way of reminder, the Court in 4chan said:

Because Plaintiffs represent that they have “no presence, infrastructure, or operations abroad,” Pls.’ Opp’n at 5; Compl. paras. 20, 24, that likely means enforcing any judgment in the United States. At that point, Plaintiffs could avail themselves of the protection of American courts.

Unless Ofcom is prepared to sail a British invasion fleet here and land ground troops, enforcement would indeed have to proceed through American courts. Which presents the following problem for Ofcom:

American courts generally decline to enforce foreign judgments that violate the United States Constitution, if indeed Plaintiffs are correct in their constitutional claims. See, e.g., Matusevitch v. Telnikoff, 877 F. Supp. 1, 4 (D.D.C. 1995) (refusing to enforce a British judgment because it contravened the First Amendment and was therefore “repugnant to the public policies of the State of Maryland and the United States”)[.]

Suffice it to say, 4chan’s constitutional arguments are correct.

The Court then added, gratuitously and sua sponte as this was not an issue which was actually briefed by either party in the case,

Finally, at the risk of gilding the lily, to the extent any foreign judgment against Plaintiffs were penal in nature, Plaintiffs may find a receptive audience before American courts regardless of the judgment’s compatibility with the United States Constitution. That is because American courts are not necessarily required to enforce foreign penal judgments[.]

Put another way, even though the Court ruled against 4chan on the sovereign immunity motion, the Court nonetheless went out of its way to communicate a message to Ofcom in this decision.

That message was: your writ doesn’t run here.

Losing the sovereign immunity motion was a price well worth paying for those dicta on enforceability and their associated deterrent value, especially considering that the only remedy 4chan sought from the D.D.C. – the one the Court couldn’t give due to sovereign immunity – was a declaration of the rights of the parties. What we got instead was the Court’s opinion as to the state of the law, inviting the parties to read between the lines; the substance of what 4chan had asked for, albeit in a different form.

Thus ended this dispute, for all practical purposes. Ofcom can’t enforce the Online Safety Act in America. Ofcom knows it, Ofcom has known it for a long time, and now, Ofcom has, finally, admitted it.

It would be a gift – to 4chan – if Ofcom decided to show up in an American court after all this, waiving sovereign immunity and thus facing the prospect of an adverse merits ruling in the process. Filing that lawsuit would be suicidal, leading to virtually certain defeat and total loss of enforcement credibility in the United States. It will almost certainly never happen, not for 4chan, and likely not for any other American target, either.

Defeat, for all practical purposes, in one matter, however, will not stop Ofcom and British parliamentarians in their continuing mission to censor the British people, and the world. Ofcom has targeted 200-ish American platforms with censorship orders; only four of those sites, all of which are my clients, refused, and only one is 4chan. The First Amendment remains very much under direct, sustained assault from foreign censorship agencies, who rely on their orders to cow U.S. companies who don’t have the stomach for a prolonged and public regulatory fight.

We have a long way to go until our fight with the foreign censors is done. We need permanent U.S. law reform to turn the tide.

The GRANITE Act, a foreign censorship shield now before both the House and Senate (H.R. 10174 / S. 5478), is one proposed legal response America could adopt. The HOMEFRONT Act, H.R. 10309, is another. Either of GRANITE or HOMEFRONT would strip sovereign immunity from foreign censors and let Americans targeted by their orders drag those agencies into federal court, where they could be held accountable for their actions. As we learn from Ofcom’s admissions today, foreign censors won’t start litigation fights they know they will lose.

What will happen next is that Ofcom is going to go back to Parliament to ask for the authority to obtain “interim business disruption measures” – i.e., more or less unilateral censorship powers to block foreign websites in the UK before starting an enforcement process, rather than after. These powers were explicitly rejected by Parliament the last time around and have even now been repudiated by Nadine Dorries, the former MP who introduced the Bill, having seen what a mess Ofcom has made of it. These powers will also be easily defeated through the use of a VPN.

They may also seek to block 4chan. My client has already priced that in and it is a price worth paying, as this will constitute the UK censoring its own people and ISPs, rather than censoring my client. The UK has the sovereign right to do that. My client has the constitutional right to decline to assist the UK in that terrible work.

The UK thus continues its authoritarian backsliding. Sorting out their own country is, ultimately, a matter for the British, and opposing the grant of new powers for Ofcom – an agency which was held off by a pair of American solos working for free – on domestic policy grounds is a task for the growing UK free speech movement to take up, with urgency.

I wish them luck in that important work. In the meantime, we Americans have plenty more work to do on this side of the pond to protect our border and prevent the British, Australian, Russian, and other foreign censorship regimes from crossing it.

items.title: The Future of CSS
items.author: soheilpro
items.summary: For the past few years, all of the major browser vendors (Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla, along with Igalia and Bocoup) have been working together on

blocks.x: For the past few years, all of the major browser vendors (Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla, along with Igalia and Bocoup) have been working together on Interop(opens in new tab), a project to improve universal browser support on web technologies. It’s been a remarkably successful effort; when a focus area gets added to Interop, it often winds up reaching near-100% support across all major browsers within a year. ✨

CSS Subgrid is a good example. Subgrid is a super-powerful extension to CSS Grid which enables entirely new layouts. It was implemented in Firefox back in 2019, but there wasn’t much movement with other browsers for years. It got added to Interop 2023, and by the end of that year, it was widely available across all modern browsers:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/_next/image/?url=%2Fimages%2Finterop-2027%2Fsubgrid-graph.png&w=1200&q=75
blocks.c: A graph showing CSS Subgrid going from only 12% of tests passing in January 2023 to 91% of tests passing by the end of the year. Safari went from 72% to 100%, Chrome/Edge went from 12% to 100%, and Firefox went from 63% to 91%

blocks.x: As we reach the end of 2026, Interop 2027 is currently being planned, and the team at Mozilla has created a ranking system(opens in new tab) for us to upvote our most-requested features. They plan on using the ranking data to decide what to include for next year’s Interop!

In this blog post, I want to dig into the top 10 features I voted for, to offer a bit of a preview of what CSS might look like within the next year. There will also be some little tips and tricks you can start using today!
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27
One of the most exciting ideas is the proposal to add functions to CSS(opens in new tab):
Copy to clipboard
If you’re familiar with JavaScript, this should feel pretty familiar. We define new functions with @function and specify the returned value with result.

There’s so much cool stuff we can do with this. Personally, the use case I’m most interested in is the ability to convert between polar and cartesian coordinates, a concept we use over and over in my Whimsical Animations course(opens in new tab):
Copy to clipboard

This feels pretty “science-fiction” to me, but it’s already implemented in Chromium browsers, and if it gets added to Interop 2027, I think there’s very good odds that it could become widely available sooner rather than later!
Link to this heading2. Bevels and squircles with corner-shape
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27

In CSS, we can use the border-radius property to round off the edges of our DOM nodes to create rounded rectangles. This property effectively adds a quarter-circle to each corner, connecting the 4 straight sides.
The corner-shape property is an exploration of alternative ways to connect the 4 sides of our DOM nodes. It provides a handful of new options:
Code Playground
Format code using Prettier
HTMLCSS
<style>
.box {
border-radius: 16px;
&.squircle {
corner-shape: squircle;
&.bevel {
corner-shape: bevel;
&.notch {
corner-shape: notch;
&.scoop {
corner-shape: scoop;
</style>
<div class="wrapper">
Round (default)
Squircle
Bevel
Notch
Scoop
Focus the editor. This will trap focus until you press Escape.Code editor:
Result
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/corner-shape-options.png
blocks.c: 5 boxes each with different corner shapes: round, squircle, bevel, notch, and scoop. Round is the default, squircle is a slightly smoother and more angled circular corner, bevel is a 45-degree diagonal corner, not is a square cutout corner, and scoop is a circular cutout corner

blocks.x: Refresh results pane
Resize editor. Use left/right arrows.

When I first heard about this property, I was most excited about squircle. If you’re not familiar, squircles are an alternative algorithm for generating rounded corners using superellipses. Apple has been making use of them for years because they produce smoother, gentler edges.

That said, after messing around with corner-shape for a while, I find myself using corner-shape: bevel a ton. It’s great for creating video game / sci-fi UIs. Here’s a little preview of a side-project I’ve been working on, with tons of corner-shape: bevel:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/_next/image/?url=%2Fimages%2Finterop-2027%2Fbeveled-corners.png&w=750&q=75
blocks.c: Screenshot of a monochromatic UI with tons of layered gray boxes. Each box has a 45-degree beveled corner.

blocks.x: We’ve technically been able to do stuff like this with clip-path or masks, but unlike those features, corner-shape actually changes the shape of the border-box. This means that our borders, outlines, and box-shadows will correctly follow the altered corner shapes!
And even though this property isn’t available in Firefox/Safari (as I write this in October 2026), I think it’s reasonable to start using it today. It’s a perfect progressive enhancement!
Link to this heading3. Infinite possibilities with border-shape
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27
In addition to corner-shape, there’s a separate proposal for border-shape(opens in new tab), which is essentially a lower-level version that allows us to draw the border ourselves.

I covered this property in depth in a recent newsletter issue, so I won’t repeat myself too much here. To summarize, border-shape lets us create whatever border shape we want using straight lines, arcs, and Bézier curves.
I used this property recently to draw this card with a big circular scoop at the top:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/_next/image/?url=%2Fimages%2Finterop-2027%2Fhegemon-card.png&w=1080&q=75
blocks.c: Screenshot of a portrait-oriented green card with a floating gold coin. The card has squircle-style corners and a big circular cutout along the top, tracing the bottom edge of the coin

blocks.x: Like corner-shape, this property changes the element’s actual border box, so borders/outlines/shadows will trace it correctly. I drew the shape I wanted and then added a white border and black outline to achieve the effect shown above!
We can even animate between differnt border shapes, like I do in this clip:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/border-shape-dynamic.mp4
You can learn a bit more about this property in my newsletter issue on the subject.
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27
I recently published a blog post on Anchor Positioning, one of the most exciting modern CSS features (which was actually prioritized in Interop 2026, and is now widely available!).

The Anchor Positioning API allows us to anchor one element to another. For example, we might anchor a floating tooltip element to its trigger, so that no matter where that trigger is on the page, the tooltip will always be connected to it.

If you’ve ever tried to solve this sort of problem yourself, you know it’s surprisingly tricky. For example, we might want our tooltip to float above the anchor, but what if the anchor is near the top of the viewport?
This is a tooltip displaying additional information about this button.
Example button
The tooltip fits comfortably.
This is a tooltip displaying additional information about this button.
Example button
The tooltip’s getting cut off!

The original Anchor Positioning API gave us most of the tools needed to solve this problem easily in CSS. It allows us to specify fallback positions; if the target element doesn’t fit above the anchor, it can flip automatically to the bottom.

The only thing missing was the ability to tell whether or not the target had flipped. We had no way to know, in CSS, whether the target element is currently sitting above or below the anchor, whether it’s using the default or fallback position. For tooltips, this is a problem because we typically want to add a little protrusion that points towards the anchor.

The “Level 2” version of the Anchor Positioning API includes a new type of container query that allows us to check whether the target element is using a fallback position or not. You can learn more about it in my Anchor Positioning blog post, or check out the Interop 2027 proposal(opens in new tab).

So honestly, I had never heard of this proposal(opens in new tab), and as far as I can tell, it isn’t implemented in any browsers. It’s not even listed on caniuse, so I can’t display one of those little widgets!
And yet, the moment I saw it, it became something I needed to have. 😂
As you might know, the inherit keyword in CSS allows us to pass a value down from the parent, even if that property isn’t typically inherited:
Code Playground
Format code using Prettier
HTMLCSS
<style>
main {
border: 3px dashed red;
p {
border: inherit;
</style>
<main>
This paragraph inherits the dashed red border!
</main>
Focus the editor. This will trap focus until you press Escape.Code editor:
Result
Refresh results pane
Resize editor. Use left/right arrows.
This is a useful little trick to reuse values, but I frequently wind up discovering that it doesn’t quite work. For example, suppose we have nested border radiuses (or is it radii?):
Code Playground
Format code using Prettier
HTMLCSS
<style>
main {
border: 2px solid red;
border-radius: 16px;
p {
border: inherit;
border-radius: inherit;
</style>
<main>
This paragraph inherits the dashed red border!
</main>
Focus the editor. This will trap focus until you press Escape.Code editor:
Result
Refresh results pane
Resize editor. Use left/right arrows.
In order for nested border radii to look correct, we need to reduce the amount of rounding on the inner radius. So I don’t exactly want to use the inherited value; I want to transform it.
That's where the proposed inherit() function comes in. It will pluck the inherited value and allow us to modify it using calc():
Copy to clipboard
Given how preliminary this feature is, I’d be a bit surprised if it makes the cut for Interop 2027. But I hope we do get this feature in the future! It seems super useful. 😄
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27
In my blog post on scroll-driven animations, we explore how we can scrub through a keyframe animation by scrolling. For example, we can use it to fade an element in as it traverses the viewport:

Scroll-driven animations were part of Interop 2026(opens in new tab), and it’s been successfully implemented across all browsers. In addition to Scroll-driven animations, however, there’s a separate proposal for scroll-triggered animations.

With scroll-triggered animations, the goal is to trigger a keyframe animation when the user scrolls to a specific point, like a proximity sensor going off. At that point, the animation runs normally over a specified duration.

We can currently implement scroll-triggered animations using the IntersectionObserver API in JavaScript, but it’s kind of a pain. It’ll be super nice when we can use CSS for both scroll-driven and scroll-triggered animations, since they each have their own use cases.
You can learn more about scroll-triggered animations in this wonderful article by Bramus(opens in new tab).
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27
I’m currently working on a top-secret project which involves a dynamic grid-based layout. Items are arranged very differently on desktop vs. mobile:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/btn-sounds-desktop.png
blocks.c: A blurry image showing a list of things on the left, a big red button in the middle, and some extra panels on the right

blocks.x: Desktop Layout
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/btn-sounds-mobile.png
blocks.c: A blurry image showing a single narrow column with a big red button, then a list of things, then some extra config panels

blocks.x: Mobile Layout

This is one of the great things about responsive CSS, but it leads to an unfortunate side effect: tab order is always based on the DOM order, not the visual order. So, if someone uses assistive technologies to navigate between elements, that navigation order will always be the same, even as the layout changes dramatically depending on screen size.

On desktop, the first visual item is that list of Redactedsounds on the left, but on mobile, the first item is that big red button. Whichever element comes first in the DOM will be the first item to receive focus, which will invariably be wrong for a percentage of our users.
Thankfully, the new reading-flow property grants us a solution to this problem, and there’s a proposal for Interop 2027(opens in new tab).
The basic idea is that we can specify that the tab order should follow one of several visual orders:
Copy to clipboard
There are values for both CSS Grid and Flexbox, and if you need even more control, the reading-order property allows us to create a custom order, sorta like tabIndex in HTML.
This property has been championed by one of my personal heroes, Rachel Andrew. You can read more about it in her blog post on reading-flow.
Link to this heading8. Keyword size animations with interpolate-size and calc-size()
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27

A long-standing pain point on the web has been the inability to animate between keyword values like auto. The interpolate-size property solves this problem, and there’s an Interop 2027 proposal(opens in new tab) for it, alongside the related calc-size() function.
The most common use case for this feature is to animate between height: 0 and height: auto, for creating collapsible accordion-type UIs:
Code Playground
Format code using Prettier
HTMLCSS
<style>
html {
interpolate-size: allow-keywords;
@supports (
interpolate-size: allow-keywords
details {
overflow: hidden;
&::details-content {
height: 0;
transition:
height 300ms,
content-visibility 300ms;
transition-behavior: allow-discrete;
&:open::details-content {
height: auto;
</style>
<details>
<summary>Click me to show/hide!</summary>
This is the hidden content which animates as it is shown/hidden. 😄
</details>

Result
Refresh results pane
Resize editor. Use left/right arrows.
The interpolate-size property is not yet supported in your browser. Here’s what it looks like in supported browsers:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/details-summary-animated.mp4

This is admittedly kind of a complex example, requiring other niche-but-well-supported CSS like transition-behavior. But the key thing is that interpolate-size: allow-keywords makes this sort of transition possible.
This proposal has been kicking around for a while now, and it’s been implemented in Chrome since 2024, so hopefully it makes it into Interop 2027!

And even though it isn’t yet available in all browsers, we can start using it today as a progressive enhancement. Just be sure to gate the transition behind a @supports query, since otherwise a brief delay will be added to unsupported browsers.
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27

One of the things that makes CSS Grid layout unique is that the grid children are positioned using rows/columns defined entirely in CSS. In every other layout mode, elements are positioned using other elements! In Table layout, for example, every grid cell has an associated <td> or <th> element.

There are a lot of upsides to CSS Grid, but one of the downsides is that it’s not as easy to add borders between grid cells. If a grid cell is empty, there’s no element to slap a border: 1px solid on!
The gap decorations proposal(opens in new tab) introduces a new set of CSS properties that will allow us to use a border-like syntax on the grid itself. Check this out:
Code Playground
Format code using Prettier
HTMLCSS
<style>
.grid {
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr);
gap: 1px;
border: 1px solid red;
/* 👇 The new feature 👇 */
rule: 1px solid red;
</style>
<div class="grid">
1
2
Focus the editor. This will trap focus until you press Escape.Code editor:
Result
Refresh results pane
Resize editor. Use left/right arrows.
The rule property is not yet supported in your browser. Here’s what it looks like in supported browsers:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/row-rule.png
blocks.c: A 3-by-3 grid with red borders between each row and column. The first two cells have a peach-colored element, the rest are empty.

blocks.x: Like border, the rule property is a shorthand property that allows us to specify the width, color, and style (dashed/dotted/solid) of the line. We can also use row-rule and column-rule if we only want to draw lines between each row or column.
In the meantime, while we wait for browsers to support gap decorations, how can we add lines between each grid cell?
I’ve been using the same workaround for many years now. Here’s what it looks like:
Code Playground
Format code using Prettier
HTMLCSS
<style>
.grid {
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr);
gap: 1px;
padding: 1px;
background-color: red;
.empty.child {
background-color: white;
</style>
<div class="grid">
1
2
Focus the editor. This will trap focus until you press Escape.Code editor:
Result
Refresh results pane
Resize editor. Use left/right arrows.
The basic idea is that the grid itself gets a background-color that matches the border we want, and we add a 1px gap so that the background peeks through between each cell.

Unfortunately, this means that we need to add a bunch of empty DOM nodes to fill each cell in the grid. It also only works if the page background is a solid color. And it’s nowhere near as flexible as the upcoming rule property is; for example, we can’t add a bit of space between the grid’s outer border and the inner grid lines.
This is just one of many techniques we explore in my comprehensive CSS course, CSS for JavaScript Developers.
Classic workaround
Current Browser Support
Supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154
Not supported in Firefox 157
Not supported in Safari 27

When working with position: sticky, have you ever wished there was a way to know whether the element was currently “stuck” or not? For example, maybe you’ve wanted to change the background color of a sticky header when it becomes stuck to the top of the viewport.

header {
position: sticky;
top: 0;
container-type: scroll-state;
@container scroll-state(stuck: top) {
.header-content {
background: var(--gray-300);
border-bottom:
1px solid var(--gray-500);
</style>

<div class="header-content">

top: 0;

to bottom,

bottom: 0;
background: linear-gradient(
to top,
black,
transparent
opacity: 0;

opacity: 1;
/* Shared styles */
&::before, &::after {
content: '';
position: absolute;
left: 0;
right: 0;
height: 50px;
pointer-events: none;

</style>

If there's the ability to scroll up, scrollable: top matches, and so we reveal the pseudo-element floating over the top of the content. When scrolled all the way up, scrollable: top no longer applies, and so the gradient is hidden.
Here’s what this looks like in supported browsers:
https://www.joshwcomeau.com/images/interop-2027/scroll-state-gradients.mp4
As we head into Interop’s 7th year, it's undeniable that the project has been a smashing success for the web. I’m so glad they keep building on this success!

I know it’s kind of a weird time right now for web developers, and many of us are wondering whether we even need to care about this kind of stuff anymore. If we’re delegating all of our work to LLMs, do we still need to keep up with the latest-and-greatest CSS features?

Personally, I think it’s more important than ever. We can’t expect LLMs to use modern CSS features when so much of their training data is years old. Most of the features I’ve shared in this post can be used today as a progressive enhancement, and if history is any guide, many of them will soon be widely available.

If we want to build the best possible user experiences, we’ll need to guide our agents to take advantage of modern web features, which requires us to know about them! This is something I dug into in a newsletter issue earlier this year: deep technical expertise remains incredibly worthwhile in the agentic era.

Finally, I’d strongly encourage you to rank your own top choices(opens in new tab)! There’s a ton of great proposals in this list, including some exciting JavaScript APIs like Temporal which didn’t make sense to include in this blog post.

Yesterday, the title The End of Education by Neil Postman called to me from my
items.text:
What is the purpose of education in the age of AGI?

October 19, 2026

Yesterday, the title The End of Education by Neil Postman called to me from my bookshelf, whispering that it might be the right book at the right time. It was. Published in 1995, it was surprisingly appropriate balm for the soul of a confused programmer and soon-to-be father.

My wife and I are expecting our first child. My economically valuable skillset – programming – suddenly feels less valuable. What shall I teach my son? And to what end?

Mr. Edison says
That the radio will supplant the teacher.
Already one may learn languages by means
Of Victrola records.
The moving picture will visualize
What the radio fails to get across.
Teachers will be relegated to the backwoods.
With fire-horses,
And long-haired women;
Or, perhaps shown in museums.
Education will become a matter
Of pressing the button.
Perhaps I can get a position at the switchboard.

– Quoted in The End of Education by Neil Postman, quoting Teachers and Machines: The Use of Technology Since 1920 by Larry Cuban

In Edison’s own words:

Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools… Our school system will be completely changed inside of ten years.

– Thomas Edison, The New York Dramatic Mirror, 1913

Back in 2013, I boldly predicted that MOOCs would upend education. Ah, my past self, you sweet summer child.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb has helped me appreciate the staying power of staying power, sometimes called The Lindy Effect. Merely staying alive implies some anti-fragility to adapt and survive. Consider that Harvard, Yale, and Princeton were founded to educate the clergy. From The End of Education:

In the Western world, beginning in the thirteenth century and for five hundred years afterward, that God was sufficient justification for the founding of institutions of learning, from grammar schools, where children were taught to read the Bible, to great universities, where men were trained to be ministers of God.

Schools survived what happened to religion. It should be no surprise that they’ve survived the radio, motion pictures, and the internet.

We typically confuse why something claims it exists, ie to glorify God, vs the forces that actually perpetuate it, which are subtler, we’d prefer not spoken aloud, and more prosaic, ie endowments, prestige, and needing someone to watch one’s kids.

It has been a surprisingly good bet that schools will continue to exist in roughly their current form for many years to come. Ironically, there also seems to be some staying power to technologists boldly (and so far incorrectly) doubting the staying power of schools! I myself have contributed to this grand tradition multiple times, and find myself at risk of doing it yet again.

Surely this time must finally be different, right? We have captured intelligence in a bottle, and you’re telling me that “Ok class, turn to page 17” and “Does anyone know how to solve for x” are still going to be around in the 2030s?

There are many shifting purposes to education, which underpin how it has survived this long. As the times change, so do its purposes shift and adapt, such as:

become a good person

become a good citizen

earn a living

make the world better

learn basic facts

I once tried to come up with a single-word purpose for education, and I landed upon the word “resourceful”, because I reasoned that if you “were able to use arbitrary resources to uncover and solve problems”, you had no more need for schooling. In the age of Google, email, and the internet, a person was educated when they could wield them. But now I see my vision of resourcefulness perfected in the AI agent and its tool loop. Maybe resourcefulness will go the way of the Dewey Decimal System which in turn supplanted memorization and an oral tradition.

Imagine education as a table held up by its many purposes. I didn’t realize how centrally important “the ability to earn a living” was for me until it started to wobble. A big reason is because I’m looking for a more objective arbiter of “good” in education. Education’s own tests and measures can feel stifling. The market offered a counterpoint. Steve Jobs and Bill Gates were college dropouts, but the market deemed them good. Now that I think of it, apparently Einstein was a mediocre student, but his contributions to science were his way out. With recent advances in AI mathematics, both of these paths to glory are under fire. Clara Collier makes similar points in her exceptional essay “After Work, We’ll Have Each Other.”

If AI takes our ability to contribute, what’s left for our children?

Neil Postman offers a few suggestions for positive purposes for education that I found heartening, not mainly for their content, but for the fact that it’s possible to make up new purposes for education and advocate for them. My favorite suggestions of Postman’s are:

Spaceship Earth – we’re all in this together; let’s take care of each other and our planet

The American Experiment – let’s revive our sense of wonder, curiosity, and responsibility about what America is and can be

The World Makers – as a student of McLuhan, Postman would be remiss if he didn’t invite students to make the tools and narratives that thereafter make us

At the risk of going too meta, I do strongly believe in Postman’s point (in his other education book, Teaching as a Subversive Activity) that “the medium is the message.” That the way we teach what we teach is often more important than the what. And likewise, I believe in Dr. Alfie Kohn’s notion that we should relate to our educational charges as humans, not objects – “doing with” vs “doing to”. Thus, I believe it may be most honest and effective to invite our children to help us craft the purpose for their education as we figure it out together.

Wish me luck.

items.title: Google open-sources TorchTPU, a native PyTorch back end for TPUs
items.author: ilreb
items.summary:
This project provides a PyTorch backend for Google's Tensor Processing Units
(TPUs), enabling users to run PyTorch models and operations on TPU devices.
items.text:
This project provides a PyTorch backend for Google's Tensor Processing Units
(TPUs), enabling users to run PyTorch models and operations on TPU devices. It
includes custom ATen kernels for various PyTorch operations, a compilation cache
for optimizing execution, and examples for distributed training and model
inference.

PyTorch ATen kernel implementation for TPU.

Compilation cache for optimized execution of XLA computations.

Support for distributed training (Data Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism).

Examples for various models (Llama, Qwen, ResNet, DLRM, minGPT, UNet).

Integration with torch.compile() for graph mode execution.

Utilities for debugging and benchmarking.

User Guide and Interactive Notebooks

A user guide is available at
https://torchtpu.readthedocs.io/. This is a
static version of the interactive notebooks. They are available in the docs
folder.

The notebooks are Marimo (similar to Jupyter). They can be run with marimo edit file.py and then you can access them in your browser. You will need to be
running this from a TPU VM, a v6e GCE instance is easiest.

The same instructions are available in the user guide linked above.

TorchTPU's Python version support policy matches
PyTorch's Release Compatibility Matrix.
Currently, Python 3.11+ is supported. See the
Python Version Support Policy for
more details.

First create a Python virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

or, with uv

uv venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Install the latest public release
(0.2.0 on PyPI) (for uv prepend
uv to all pip commands):

pip install torch_tpu==0.2.0 --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

Wheels can be built via:

bazel build --config=wheel_common //ci/wheel:torch_tpu_wheel

All OSS Bazel builds default to optimized mode (-c opt) automatically via
.bazelrc. Unoptimized builds (-c fastbuild, -c dbg) can degrade
performance and are not used for wheel builds. If you are developing or
debugging C++ code and explicitly want an unoptimized wheel, pass
--//:allow_unoptimized_wheel=True:

bazel build -c dbg --config=wheel_common //ci/wheel:torch_tpu_wheel \
--//:allow_unoptimized_wheel=True

--config=wheel_common is required, and the build fails at build time without
it. The config sets --//:wheel_build=True, which routes the shared XLA/MLIR
backend through the torch_version-reset transition so that pywrap factors it
into a single libxla_base.so; built without the flag, every per-version common
ships its own copy of the backend and the resulting wheel aborts on import torch with duplicate static registrations.

remote executor. If you do not have RBE credentials, append --config=no_rbe to
strip those flags back out:

--config=wheel_common, because the later config is the one that wins for the
remote-cache and remote-executor flags they both set.

cd <path_to_repo>
python -m venv .venv; source .venv/bin/activate
# The extra-index-url provides the CPU version of torch rather than the default CUDA build.
pip install ../bazel-bin/ci/wheel/*.whl --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

pass --extra-index-url as shown above or install the CPU build separately.

See the

for more install instructions

However you install it, add it's location to PATH.

To verify the install, run bazel info in the repo's root directory:

It should print information about the repo without errors.

For C++ code navigation, it is recommended to use VSCode with
clangd extension.
Relying on a
compilation database
generated from Bazel action graph, clangd is able to
enrich the editor with various smart features, including code completions, go-to
definitions, etc.

code --install-extension llvm-vs-code-extensions.vscode-clangd
# Uninstall Microsoft C++ extensions to avoid interference.

items.title: SlopCodeBench 10/2026 – Opus 5.5, Astra wins overall, xhigh considered harmful
items.author: dhorthy
items.summary:
SlopCodeBench update 10/2026 - Opus 5.5 update, Astra improves by 1.5% over gpt-5.5, xhigh considered harmful

October 15, 2026 - Dex Horthy w/ contributions
items.text:
SlopCodeBench update 10/2026 - Opus 5.5 update, Astra improves by 1.5% over gpt-5.5, xhigh considered harmful

October 15, 2026 - Dex Horthy w/ contributions from Gabe Orlanski

NOTE: This is Part I of our October 2026 writeup: the Q4 state of the slop. Gabe and the SlopCodeBench team will share their analysis and a more qualitative deep dive into slop patterns in Part II.

For my previous writeups on SlopcodeBench, see benchmarking-opus-5-on-slop-code-bench.md and benchmarking-sol-fable-kimi-on-slop-code-bench.md. Both include deeper dives on the core structure of SCB and how each of its challenges is broken into checkpoints.

In May, the last time SCB was published, gpt-5.5 got a 14.8% strict pass rate on slopcodebench. This month, I ran the frontier models through the same campaigns, and the highest scorer was gpt-6 astra, hitting 16.3%.

While the benchmark reports several different pass rates, the one we focus on is strict pass rate - in how many checkpoints did the model pass every test case while still passing all regression tests the frontier models we tested here had strict pass rates in the 12.2-16.3% range:

Opus 5.5

Fable 5.1

SOL 6 and 6.1

Astra

GLM 5.3

For comparison, the benchmark also reports a "core pass rate" which is less strict, which lands in the 65.8-74.0% pass rate for these models.

One interesting thing here that I'll dig into - medium effort performed better than XHigh for some newer models. XHigh costs 2.11-4.22x as much as Medium in the three complete pairs, and most notably, opus 5.5 did BETTER on medium effort than on xhigh

Over the past few months, I ran subsets of the bench. I started with three problems, then tried six. This time: 36 problems and 196 checkpoints per setting. Since we used a subset before, we can't use the earlier subsets to measure improvement or decline. The full benchmark lets us compare these results with the official research findings. It also means while the 30% fable 5 score from the latter of those two is interesting, its not comparable here, because it only covers 6 out of 36 problems.

SlopCodeBench gives a coding agent a problem in stages. It writes a program, gets new requirements, and changes the existing code. Later checkpoints test both new behavior and old behavior.

The idea here is that this maps more onto how software is really built - with unclear and evolving requirements during the course of the build.

For folks who want to try to repro these findings: I used the pinned v1.0 catalog, the stock just-solve prompt, seed 42, the any-case runner pass policy, and Docker with Python 3.12 and uv.

I ran each model and effort setting once. Each checkpoint builds on the code from earlier checkpoints. Some problems have more checkpoints than others. Each checkpoint counts equally toward the pass rate, so problems with more checkpoints have more weight.

Core vs. Strict pass rates

Strict: every test category passes, including Regression.

Core: all tests in a nonempty Core category pass. For example, if a model fails checkpoint 2, it can still get a core pass for a later checkpoint, even if the ck2 tests remain failing.

Strict passes: 24-32 of 196. Core passes, including strict: 129-145. The tinted portion isn't extra strict success.

code quality findings - blurry

First - the models left a ton of junk and scratch code while working. My first reaction was to remove the random temp files from the quality scores. But I chatted with gabe and he made a good point: the benchmark should measure how much garbage models leave in the codebase. If we're not reading the code, we need to measure it. Tests, scratch code, and generated copies probably shouldn't get a free pass just because they aren't the main program.

I did use a fixed list of folder names to exclude installed packages, virtual environments, and caches from both analyses.

The main results analyze all leftover code. For comparison, we also calculate the same metrics after removing a fixed list of temporary and generated files. That lets us see how much the cleanup changes the numbers. The rules and the actual difference are below.

These figures cover the same 28 problems for all ten completed runs, not all 36 problems. The scanner couldn't fully measure some files in eight problems (more on that in gabe's update later), so we left those problems out for every model.

Some high level details on how we compute "what % of this code triggers at least one slop rule":

The scanner flags slop patterns and repeated code within each file.

"Coverage" is the share of source lines flagged by those checks.

We count each line only once, even if several checks flag it.

A check can flag a whole function without every line being a problem.

We total the flagged lines and source lines across all 28 problems, then divide to get the percentage. Larger programs therefore have more weight. In the earlier posts, we averaged each problem's percentage instead.

Opus XHigh has the lowest slop percentage at 77.75%, versus 94.25% for Opus Medium. Interestingly, once again, the xhigh version has fewer strict passes: 25 versus 28.

while Opus 5.5 Medium had more strict passes, Opus 5.5. XHigh wrote code that was close to ~5x cleaner.

It is possible that this is because newer models come with new / different slop patterns, and the paper's original battery of 200+ linters is focused on a set of hand-curated patterns derived from agent-authored PRs in the months preceding the original publication in march 2026 and the v1.1 in may 2026. These new models may produce new maintainability anti-patterns that we haven't built linters for yet (more on that in Gabe's follow up post).

Opus Medium leaves the most code, even after filtering. We don't remove all tests.

For the filtered score, we leave out folders named _work, tmp, temp, scratch, generated, build, or dist, plus *_pb2.py and *_pb2_grpc.py files. We use the same rules for every run. We don't guess whether code looks generated or exclude tests as a group. In these runs, the filter only removed _work files: 45 files and 41,265 source lines, all from Opus Medium's final dynamic_buffer code. Its total drops from 216,881 to 175,616 source lines, and slop-presence drops to 92.90%. It still ranks most-frequent on slop presence. The filter changes nothing for the other models.

Fable has the lowest mean complexity, 3.57; GPT-6 SOL Medium has the highest, 11.70. Functions and methods each get one vote.

As you might expect, splitting code into more helper functions can lower average complexity without making the code easier to change. Less code isn't always better either.

There's a ton more metrics and I'm excited to get Gabe's take on the more qualitative side of these outputs.

The full benchmark is hard in a way that matters to me: the agents get the main behavior right much more often than they keep all tested behavior working as requirements change.

We're getting better at maintaing a codebase over time (14.8% to 16.3% during may->september), but not as fast as anyone would have you believe. I think we'll be keeping the lights on for a while to come.

NOTE: This is Part I of our October 2026 writeup: the Q4 state of the slop. Gabe and the SlopCodeBench team will share their analysis and a more qualitative deep dive into slop patterns in Part II.

blocks.x: Opus Medium leaves the most code, even after filtering. We don't remove all tests.

For the filtered score, we leave out folders named _work, tmp, temp, scratch, generated, build, or dist, plus *_pb2.py and *_pb2_grpc.py files. We use the same rules for every run. We don't guess whether code looks generated or exclude tests as a group. In these runs, the filter only removed _work files: 45 files and 41,265 source lines, all from Opus Medium's final dynamic_buffer code. Its total drops from 216,881 to 175,616 source lines, and slop-presence drops to 92.90%. It still ranks most-frequent on slop presence. The filter changes nothing for the other models.

blocks.c: Functions and methods alongside callable-weighted mean complexity. Fable has 8,967 callables and mean complexity 3.57; GPT-6 SOL Medium has 1,083 and mean complexity 11.70.

blocks.x: Fable has the lowest mean complexity, 3.57; GPT-6 SOL Medium has the highest, 11.70. Functions and methods each get one vote.
As you might expect, splitting code into more helper functions can lower average complexity without making the code easier to change. Less code isn't always better either.
There's a ton more metrics and I'm excited to get Gabe's take on the more qualitative side of these outputs.
The full benchmark is hard in a way that matters to me: the agents get the main behavior right much more often than they keep all tested behavior working as requirements change.

We're getting better at maintaing a codebase over time (14.8% to 16.3% during may->september), but not as fast as anyone would have you believe. I think we'll be keeping the lights on for a while to come.
NOTE: This is Part I of our October 2026 writeup: the Q4 state of the slop. Gabe and the SlopCodeBench team will share their analysis and a more qualitative deep dive into slop patterns in Part II.

items.title: Feds suspect ransom negotiator ran ShinyHunters extortion site
items.author: Bender
items.summary: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two
items.text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

SHINYWIRE

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

GHOSTBYTE

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

CONFLICTING INTERESTS

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
